summary.text: An amorphous solid is a solid that lacks the long-range order that is a characteristic of a crystal.
Examples include glasses, metallic glasses and certain plastics and polymers, none of which can be described by repeating a finite unit cell.
They still show localized order on small length scales, and how a liquid freezes into one, the glass transition, is considered an important unsolved problem in physics.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Greek a, meaning without, plus morphe, meaning shape or form

facts.label: Examples
facts.value: Glasses, metallic glasses, and certain plastics and polymers

facts.label: Short-range order
facts.value: Extends only to the nearest neighbor shell, 1-2 atomic spacings

facts.label: Diffraction
facts.value: Broad, diffuse peaks, not the strong Bragg diffraction of crystals

items.prompt: A scientist tries to describe a piece of glass by repeating one small box of atoms through the material, as is done for a crystal. Why does it fail?

options.label: No long-range regularity exists, so no finite repeating unit fits
Glass atoms are too heavy to fit in a box
Glass atoms keep moving between boxes
Glass has no atoms in any pattern, even over a few neighbors

items.explain: Amorphous materials have no long-range regularity and cannot be described by the repetition of a finite unit cell.

items.prompt: An amorphous solid has no long-range order. Do its atoms have any order at all?

options.label: No, its atoms are placed completely at random
Yes, and the order runs just as far as in a crystal
Yes, but only on small scales, around a few neighbors
No, because order only exists in liquids

items.explain: Amorphous materials lack long-range order but show localized order on small length scales, reaching the nearest neighbor shell.

items.prompt: A lab fires X-rays at a crystal and at a piece of plastic. How do the patterns differ?

options.label: The crystal gives broad, diffuse peaks, the plastic gives strong sharp ones
The crystal gives strong sharp diffraction, the plastic gives broad, diffuse peaks
Both give identical sharp patterns
The plastic gives no pattern at all

items.explain: Crystalline materials show strong Bragg diffraction, while amorphous materials give broad and diffuse peaks.

items.prompt: Physicists measure how an amorphous solid and a crystalline solid conduct heat at very low temperatures. What do they find?

options.label: Both behave the same way, because temperature is what matters
The crystalline solid behaves oddly, while the amorphous one is plain
Neither conducts heat at all
The amorphous solid behaves very differently, in ways called anomalous

items.explain: Low-temperature properties of amorphous solids are conventionally called anomalous, being very different from those of crystalline solids.

items.prompt: A researcher counts how many atoms lie at each distance from one chosen atom, to learn about local order. What is this analysis called?

options.label: Radial distribution function analysis of the atoms
Bragg peak analysis of sharp, repeating crystal planes
Unit cell repetition across a large piece
Latent heat measurement during cooling

items.explain: Radial distribution function analysis measures the number of atoms found at varying radial distances from an arbitrary reference atom.

items.prompt: A compound exists as both a crystal and a glassy solid. Are the glassy form's building blocks totally different from the crystal's?

options.label: Yes, they always are completely different
Yes, because glassy solids have no building blocks
Not necessarily; they can be similar, but without long-range regularity
No, because the arrangement is just as regular as in the crystal

items.explain: Amorphous materials have structural blocks that can be similar to the crystalline phase's units, but no long-range regularity exists.
